speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But faced with an unknown and dangerous virus, governments around the world concluded that this was the best way to stave off a viral invasion.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It also affected many other sectors – aerospace, tourism, hospitality, entertainment, attractions, retail, our taxi and private hire car drivers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But what is most worrying is the longer term impact on our entire economy.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Our aviation hub status is essential, even existential, to the health of the Singapore economy, to our jobs and to our future.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I have described our airport as a lung of Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Just as a lung takes in oxygen and vitalises every part of the human body, the airport connects Singapore with the outside world and energises every sector of our economy.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When a company puts a significant investment in Singapore, one key reason for them to do that is our superior air connectivity, because that means their customers, suppliers, partners and key executives, can travel in and out of Singapore easily.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They can come from any part of the world, come to Singapore and then connect on to another part of the world.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Our status as an air hub makes that possible.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: However, the longer our borders remain closed, the greater the risk of losing our air hub status and our attractiveness as a place to invest and to create jobs because of those investments.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The status quo is therefore not sustainable for us.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We cannot just wait around for a vaccine, which may take a year or two before it becomes widely available.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Even then, we do not know if the vaccine will work as expected.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We need to take proactive steps to revive the Changi Air Hub, as a top national priority.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Saktiandi and Mr Melvin Yong asked how we would achieve that.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked a similar question for the next sitting which I will answer today.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, I will give first an update on the current situation in the aviation sector; second, I will explain what has changed from the time we closed our borders in March 2020 until now, what has changed; and third, finally, what are the steps we will take to try to revive our air hub.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, let me first give the House an update of the current situation.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The numbers are stark because Singapore has no domestic air travel.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If we include cargo flights, it is higher, at 17% of total flight volume.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We were the seventh busiest airport in the world for international passenger traffic.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Two key companies in the aviation sector are facing a deep crisis.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They are Singapore Airlines (SIA) and Changi Airport Group (CAG).

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: SIA recorded its largest ever quarterly loss on record in the first quarter of Fiscal Year 2020.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is trying its best to reduce cash burn, preserve core capabilities and explore all ways to generate revenue.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Unfortunately, the SIA Group had to make the difficult decision to rationalise its workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The recently concluded agreement with SIA’s pilot union for pilots to take deeper salary cuts, enabled the SIA Group to reduce the number of retrenchments from 2,400 to 2,000.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, all in all it is about 3,900 jobs rationalised either through non-filling of vacancies, early retirement or retrenchments in the SIA Group – 3,900 jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Without the recent major recapitalisation exercise, there would not be an SIA today.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is far from being out of the woods.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: One of the initiatives SIA considered recently to generate some revenue and get more pilots to do actual flying, was a flight to nowhere.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Dennis Tan and Assoc Prof Jamus Lim asked if MOT would support this.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It has now become a moot point, because SIA has decided to scrap the idea.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Whichever way SIA had decided, MOT would always try our best to support our national carrier in times like this.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But what I will not contemplate is to impose on them an environment tax at this time, as Assoc Prof Jamus Lim indicated in his question, because that will just worsen the crisis for SIA.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: With low passenger volume and flights, the amount of service charges it is collecting from airlines and passengers is miniscule.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Shops and restaurants at the airport are seeing far fewer customers; many shops have closed.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: CAG is also dipping into its reserves, while preserving cash and retaining its core capabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa asked about the plan for Terminal 5.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is a very large-scale project undertaken by CAG.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Government will continue to support SIA, CAG and other companies in the aviation sector as much as we can.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But the most meaningful support we can give to our aviation companies is to restore passenger traffic and revive our air hub, in a safe and controlled manner.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We must recognise that compared to six months ago, when we closed our borders, the situation has changed, in a few very significant ways.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First, the virus situation in Singapore – both in the community and in the foreign worker dormitories – is largely under control.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The number of new cases in the community has remained stable at an average of one case per day in the last two weeks.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Thanks to the hard work of our healthcare staff, we have had no fatalities resulting from complications due to COVID-19 infection since mid-July.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Our fatality rate is also one of the lowest in the world.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Thankfully, for many weeks now, we have not had any patients admitted to ICU due to COVID-19 infection or its complications.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Members have heard all these updates before, but I thought I would repeat them anyway because this track record matters greatly to countries and regions seeking partners to restore aviation links.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The second major thing that has changed is our testing capacity.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: COVID-19 testing capacity is no longer a major constraint.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Back in March 2020, we could only conduct about 2,000 tests a day and they had to be reserved for critical public health purposes such as testing high-risk symptomatic individuals.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: At that time, closing our borders was the only way to slow down the import of the virus and keep Singaporeans safe.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For returning Singaporeans and residents, we subjected them to a lengthy 14-day Stay-Home Notice (SHN) – and usually "Plus".

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It means a Stay-Home Notice, plus you stay in a hotel and not at home.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, it is a lengthy 14-day "SHN Plus" invented by Minister Gan to ensure that they were free from the virus before allowing them to mingle with the rest of the community.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To give this a further boost, we will also be leveraging the private sector to develop commercial testing capacity.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: At the same time, testing technology is advancing.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There are now promising tests with quicker turnarounds while maintaining acceptable test sensitivity.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For example, DSO and A*STAR have developed the Resolute test kit.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It halves the time needed to process and analyse patient samples in the lab from two to two and a half hours to between one and one and a half hours.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There are also trials for less intrusive tests using deep throat saliva – but you must know how to spit – and efforts to develop rapid test kits such as antigen and breathalyser tests that can deliver results on the spot – in a few minutes – without having to send the samples to a laboratory for processing.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We are watching this space very carefully and with great interest.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And we will deploy these tests where practicable.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: With high-sensitivity tests, we can now filter out the virus at the border – better still, before the traveller boards the plane – and significantly mitigate the risk of importing and spreading the virus in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Testing is therefore the key to unlock air travel.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: With COVID-19 around for a while, the emerging international practice is to get tested before travel – not different from us going through security, having our bags checked before we board the plane.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: A third key change since March is tracing capability.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have scaled up our ability to quickly identify and isolate new cases and their close contacts.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When we had our first COVID-19 case in January, we relied entirely on human contact tracers to manually retrace a patient's steps.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, technologies such as SafeEntry, the TraceTogether app and tokens complement the work of human contact tracers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We can therefore quickly identify and isolate people who have come into contact with a confirmed patient.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This helps to reduce the risk of any community outbreak.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For example, the European Union has designated countries whose residents can visit Europe.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The United Kingdom – the UK – has recently exempted travellers from Singapore from their 14-day quarantine when you arrive.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Vietnam is restoring scheduled passenger flights to several cities.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Hong Kong has announced its intention to negotiate travel bubble arrangements with several countries, including Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The key is to make sure we stay safe – we can manage the risks while we open up aviation.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have gone through quite a bit – including a painful circuit breaker – to arrive at the stable situation we have today.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have seen how a second wave has broken out in other countries and regions.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In some cities, in some countries, they are going back to a lockdown again.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As of 5 October 2020, the United Arab Emirates had an infection incidence rate of about nine per 100,000 population per day and for Turkey, about two per 100,000 population per day.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Singapore – we are at 0.1 per 100,000 population per day.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I think there is a recovery and risk trade-off and we can learn from each other in managing the risks of opening up.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But as I just described, because conditions have changed over the past months, the trade-off is not as stark as before.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For Members who are hoping that I am about to announce some air travel resumption and possible December holiday destinations, I am sorry I will disappoint you.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The fact is that borders are still closed for most parts of the world.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Some countries such as Germany only allow business travellers from Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And to the best of my knowledge, only a handful of countries – such as the US, the UK, Turkey, the Maldives – allow general travellers from Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We cannot control what other countries want to do with their borders but we can control ours – to welcome back visitors, bring back jobs, revive our air hub safely.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: How we do this safely can be a useful reference point for other countries and perhaps even catalyse some safe opening around the world.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It will be a difficult and gradual climb out of a very deep abyss.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But climb we must, and we will do the following.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First, we will continue to pursue Reciprocal Green Lane arrangements with partner countries or regions.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These are restricted to a small group of essential business and official travellers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They will be subject to pre-departure and on-arrival tests to ensure they do not carry the virus.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Further, they will have controlled itineraries to minimise any residual risk of community spread.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As an air hub, about a quarter of our passenger volume at Changi are transfers, meaning the passengers do not clear immigration and are using Changi Airport as an interchange to get to their final destinations.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked for the number of such transfer passengers at Changi Airport today.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But this is still a small fraction of what we used to serve.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have put in place robust safeguards and no Singaporean has become ill as a result of these transfers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The third thing we will do – we should be prepared to lift our border restrictions to countries and to regions with comprehensive public health surveillance systems and comparable incidence rates to Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That means we are of the same risk profile, which is low.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: At the same time, when we do so, we should also lift our travel advisory for Singapore residents travelling to these countries and regions.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Purely from an infection risk point of view, the risk of a traveller from these places carrying the virus when they arrive at Changi Airport is no higher than that of a Singaporean resident coming from Jurong or Sembawang because we are of the same incidence rate and same risk profile.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But as a precaution, we will subject these travellers to a COVID-19 test to ensure they are free from the virus.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In this way, we can safely lift our border restrictions for these countries and regions and welcome their travellers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Their governments will decide if and when to reciprocate for travellers from Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Once they do that, aviation links between us would have been restored.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We do not expect big numbers in the short term because these countries currently discourage or restrict travel for their residents.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Notwithstanding this, such unilateral opening is still meaningful because it is like a standing invitation.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Although the other countries are not ready to lift their restrictions now, Singapore can be top of mind when they are ready eventually.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Recently, it unilaterally allowed Singaporeans to travel there without a quarantine.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Many of our students actually went to their universities as a result.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Once their infection rate falls and becomes comparable to ours, we will likely lift restrictions quickly, which will effectively restore air travel between our countries.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Our domestic market is not a big bargaining chip.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Instead, what we need to have is a mindset of generosity required of a hub.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is why when we were building up Changi Airport in the 1980s, we opened up our skies unilaterally.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is also why decades ago, we removed tariffs unilaterally for all countries.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Yet, many countries chose to negotiate with us for Air Services Agreements and Free Trade Agreements – because our partners know that by connecting to Singapore, they connect with the rest of the world.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They chose to deal with Singapore because it is strategic to do so.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Air Travel Bubbles are not the same as Reciprocal Green Lanes that I mentioned just now, which are for official and essential business travel only.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Air Travel Bubbles are for general travellers and have no requirements for a controlled itinerary.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We also require travellers to apply for an Air Travel Pass before their journeys, to allow us to plan for their arrivals, and if need be, throttle down the numbers, or reduce the quota if the epidemic situation changes.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We hope to commence discussions with Hong Kong and other partners soon.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Multi-Ministry Task Force will explore other practical schemes.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is especially important for travellers from countries which are economically important to us, but with higher infection rates.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There are ways to facilitate these travellers to come to Singapore while managing the risk of virus transmission.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Many stakeholders and members of public have written to us with very well thought-through and sensible ideas and we are studying them carefully.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In particular, we recognise that the requirement of having to serve a full 14-day Stay Home Notice or SHN in a hotel, will deter most travellers from wanting to come to Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, we have to facilitate the visits without such an onerous restriction.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We can segregate them from the rest of the community, a process that we call "bubble wrapping", and we can closely track their movements while they are here.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This will benefit not just business travellers important to our economy, but a range of people who need to come to Singapore for various purposes, such as compassionate reasons or to re-unite with a long-separated partner.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In the near future, if you have the virus under control and infection rates are as low as Singapore's, you are welcome to visit us, but travellers will be subject to a COVID-19 test, as a precaution.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If you are from a place where infection rates are higher than Singapore, you can also visit us, so long as you agree to conditions such as testing, segregation and tracing.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Task Force will be studying these approaches and developing the schemes.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Earlier in the year, we had to close our borders to keep Singaporeans safe.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But as we learn to control the virus and testing becomes much less of a constraint, the trade-off between health and economic needs, between lives and livelihoods, is no longer so stark, and the two do not have to be at odds.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Eventually, when there is a widely available and effective vaccine, air travel will resume.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But in the meantime, we will have to learn to live with the virus – taking sensible precautions, while earning a living, and keeping hopes for our future alive.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We did that when we emerged from the circuit breaker in June and we have been bringing back our community and social life, step by step.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have been restoring school life for our children, activity by activity, and made sure throughout that process, that our children stay safe and they did not lose their school year.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We did not rush, but neither did we baulk at what we need to do to regain our normal lives and livelihoods.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It will be the same with our international borders, to open up step-by-step, carefully, safely and steadily.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When Terminal 1 opened in 1981, it opened up a whole new world and brought prosperity undreamt of in generations past.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, the skies remain key to our economic survival.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We must open up slowly, carefully, and holding each other accountable for our collective safety.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I hope to have the support of all Members of this House, and all Singaporeans, for this critical endeavour, so as to take our place in the world once again and to start building our future as we once did.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I have three clarifications that I wish to seek from Minister.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: First of all, I do understand the recovery and risk trade-off that Minister mentioned.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I think we all mindful of it, especially with the incidence risk that comes along with opening up the country.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My first question is, the Minister mentioned about the testing technology improving and there are plans for Air Travel Bubbles, ATBs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My first question is regarding bilateral and regional arrangements with ASEAN, for example.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can the Minister share with us how are the deliberations in the plans going ahead or the task force's deliberations with ASEAN for example, in opening up our regional air travel between ASEAN countries going forward, as testing technology improves?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The second question, Minister mentioned about the logistics and cargo volume that has improved two times – I think if I am not mistaken, I heard two times, it has ramped up two times.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My question is in the interim, as we see more Scoot planes on the tarmac, as we drive past Changi, PIE and towards the end, we see Scoot planes there – is there is a possibility of ramping up our logistics and cargo volume even further, in the interim.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Particularly, because you probably might want to get the core capabilities of our aviation sector built up in the interim, as we as we wait for some of these technologies to improve or for ATBs or arrangements with other countries.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My third question is in relation to my Parliamentary Question, in post-COVID, what are our plans for the medium and longer terms.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Whether the Minister can share with us any infrastructure, strategies or plans to put us in a good stead post-COVID – I am not sure whether COVID-19 will end next year – beyond one year, two years or three, four, five years.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How Singapore can take this opportunity to put us in a better stead beyond one year ahead?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, between EU member states, they signed an agreement, they agreed for free movement between different citizens of EU member states.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Even so, between EU Schengen member states, they impose border restrictions on each other.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, Schengen means that you do not have to apply for a visa to travel from say France to Germany, but between the countries, they impose border measures.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I asked some of my European friends, what are the border measures and they said, "It is too complicated to explain.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I went to the website – EU member state has a separate border restriction.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think practically this is what is happening – and in ASEAN, it will be the same.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, that is one thing that went up in aviation despite COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But bear in mind, even during pre-COVID-19 times, cargo flights were only 4% of total flights.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, you cannot restore aviation just by banking on cargo.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Further, cargo flights ferry non-living things, and in the end, aviation is about people-to-people linkages – Singaporeans connecting with people from around the world.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Therefore, we still have to work on as hard as we can.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As Members know, we have T5, and our terminals are going through upgrading as well, so we are not short of infrastructure plans.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: What we need now is not so much the hardware, but the software of being able to open up our borders, welcome travellers to and fro but do so safely.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It will be in infrastructure such as testing capacity, such as people who can do the tests, such as adopting new, novel testing methods including rapid test kits that allow us to open up safely.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: A reminder – let us keep to two clarifications.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I am just wondering if he would be able to clarify the thinking behind why in his Statement, he mentioned that he would not consider an environmental tax because it would impose clear costs on the economic viability of SIA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I mention this because, of course, the burden of the tax as economists understand it, really falls on either the consumer or the producer, depending in large part on the intensity with which the demand or supply responds to price – what economists call an elasticity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, it is entirely possible that it does not impose an immediate concern on the viability, the economic viability, if SIA is able to pass on the cost.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The second question is, I wonder whether it is possible to consider mechanisms where the environmental needs of both the country and the world need not be a casualty to business considerations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: By which I mean we can think of innovative ways, for example, if you have a flight to nowhere – of course as the Minister mentioned a moot point right now – it could well be the case that this tax could be funded by savings on berthing rights.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And hence, ultimately the cost of a ticket need not actually rise.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, I am wondering if I could get clarifications on those.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think all these considerations can be done if there had been no COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There has been some discussion in ICAO, in the EU, in the international community.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But I think the basic answer, the simple answer is this: we are in a crisis.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And SIA is doing whatever it can to preserve cash.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And therefore, we need to help SIA preserve as much cash as it can.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If I were to do that, I think there is a Chinese saying, "落井下石".

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I would have made the situation much worse for SIA.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It means "someone fell into the well and you throw a stone to make the situation worse".

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, let us be very careful about that.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When things resume, the international conversation will go on, on whether there should be an environmental tax.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: As I hear him describe some of the things that we need to do – to have the Reciprocal Green Lane, Controlled Itinerary, the various testings, the monitoring and surveillance as well – it gives me a sense that there would be a lot of costs to be added on as well, including for the airlines when they have to fly planes that are not as full, and not to mention that the air tickets that the airlines sell would not be cheap as well, may not be that affordable.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, I want to ask the Minister from a cost-revenue standpoint, does it make sense, does it clear the break-even point for us to resume travel, given this environment?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The second question is, during this COVID-19 situation, there were quite a number of airlines that have actually moved out of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: They hub somewhere else or they find a cheaper location.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, I want to ask the Minister whether when we resume, let us say, when the air travel comes back, are we confident of bringing these major airlines back to Singapore, to hub in Singapore again?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But, at the same time, be mindful too that supply has greatly been reduced.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, just to restore some demand, we believe there are passengers who are prepared to travel.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: You can just speak to your friends – Singaporeans who have not travelled for the whole year and now you tell them, you can pay a bit more, you can visit XX country or region – I think they will be quite happy to try to do so.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Some are getting cabin fever and Singaporeans love to travel.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, I think the latent demand is there.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think we need to unlock it through the methods I mentioned earlier.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As to whether major airlines will come back, that is why we need to start taking steps, as I had mentioned, to start signalling that we are determined to hold on to our status as an air hub.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I just met a senior executive of a regional airline.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: He actually flew to Singapore, did his 14-day SHN Plus in order to meet some of us and he met me for half an hour with a clear message, "Please open up aviation again because our airlines want to come back to Singapore".

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, I think we are still top of mind for many of the airlines but we have to start taking steps to open up our borders.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: First, why has Changi Airport's passenger rank dropped from seventh place to 58th place when the crisis is global and has affected other air hubs in US and Europe far more than in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: So, how did these 51 cities overtake Singapore and what lessons are we drawing from them?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Why are they not all tested on arrival and is testing capacity a factor?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And lastly, regarding green lanes and pre-departure tests conducted in originating countries, how can we be sure that the test results are reliable, especially for countries where corruption is rife and cheating is commonplace?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Sorry, can the Member repeat the second question?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I understand that many incoming arrivals are currently placed on SHN up to 12 to 14 days before their first PCR test.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: So, why are they not all tested on arrival and is testing capacity a reason for this?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I invite the Co-chairs of the Multi-Ministry Taskforce or MTF, to chime in, if necessary.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Why is the drop in Singapore's passenger traffic so drastic?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We do not have domestic travel, like the US.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The drop, I concede, is on international travel.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But if you are a big country, China or US, you have a much bigger population who is flying out and not just flying within the country and that generates international traffic, which is why there is a certain cushion.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For us, as a small domestic market, the numbers are more stark.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: SHN, 14 days – the simple answer is this.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: What the Member mentioned about SHN 14 days, they refer to other individuals and they are undergoing their 14-day SHN, then they get their test at the end of the service of the SHN.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As for green lanes, perhaps I will ask Minister Gan or Mr Lawrence Wong to answer this.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Speaker, thank you for allowing me to chime in.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: When they come in, they may have been infected and if we test them on the spot on arrival, it may not be detected.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: That is why we put them within the SHN or SHN Plus for the whole duration of the incubation period and we test them at the end.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: And if they are still negative, that means they are past the incubation period and they are still negative, we can then allow them to go into the community.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: If we test them on the first day, the test is not going to be effective because he may still be within his incubation period.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: And you, nonetheless, have to test them again at the end of 14 days.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: And that is why instead of repeated testing, we decided that for those that require SHN because of whatever risk profile that we have decided on, they should be tested at the end of their SHN period.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I like to first declare my interest as an employee of the Changi Airport Group.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Currently, there are different travel schemes and swab and isolation protocol upon arrival for travellers – some 14 days' isolation, some seven days and some zero, for example, Australia and Brunei in the latest case.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Pre-COVID, I believe China has the highest travel volume into Singapore, so if we can actually reduce that number of days for SHN, that will reduce the deterrence for travellers to enter into Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But what I mentioned earlier about unilateral opening is better than reducing SHN from 14 days.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Because these countries have incidence rates and risk profile that are similar to or better than Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Like I had mentioned, when you have similar risk profiles, technically, there is actually no need for a test, because someone from those countries coming to Singapore – is not different from someone from Jurong or Sembawang or Bedok going to Changi Airport – same risk profile.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But out of an abundance of caution, we still administer a post-arrival test and once negative, they are free to move about, there is no need for SHN.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, I think right now it is not the time to simplify rules or reduce requirements and then apply generally.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is not the time to do that.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Now, what we need to do is to understand every single country or region, understand the risk profile and customise our approach for travellers from each of these countries or region, which is what we are doing.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: It does provide us with a clearer overview of the challenges and our strategic directions towards systematic recovery of our aviation sector.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: According to the latest flight schedules published by the SIA Group, SIA and SilkAir are gradually increasing the number of flights they operate.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Flights to Brunei, Japan and the Maldives are scheduled to be reinstated by the end of the year.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Flights for some existing routes which include Australia, France and the UK will also increase.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I like to ask if these business decisions by the SIA Group are linked to the Government's on-going negotiations on Reciprocal Travel Arrangements.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Residents have asked why SIA continues to operate flights to countries that we currently cannot travel to.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: My follow-up question is whether the Government has plans to aid the recovery of SIA in the event of a prolonged COVID-19 pandemic situation.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: So, instead of, "落井下石", I would like to ask how we can remove as many rocks and pebbles so that our SIA can soar once again.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This House has sat through many Budget speeches by Deputy Prime Minister Heng.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And I recall him mentioning many, many times all the recovery packages and help that we are giving to the aviation sector; and companies such as SIA often benefit from the top tier of the support.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, indeed, we are doing whatever we can to help our national carrier.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As for increasing the number of flights, SIA make partly their own commercial decisions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: On the other hand, there are some flights, although the load factor is low, but they are flying anyway to maintain what they call Minimum Connectivity Network, because you have got to be present in those markets and be in touch with your customers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Even though demand is low, you just need to be there.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is just the nature of the business.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, it is a combination – both because of Enhanced Aviation Support Package as well as SIA's own commercial decisions that it is increasing the number of flights.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And I just want to state that whatever that goes through air travel, that revenue goes through not only just SIA but goes through the ground-handling crew, goes through the guys at Changi Airport, goes through the taxi drivers, the Grab drivers and all the way till the monkeys at the Zoo, when we are looking at that revenue spend.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: So, I agree that there is still air travel demand.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In fact, in the industry – and I would like to declare that I work in the aerospace industry – as we are commissioning new equipment and new machinery, we are still asking from engineers from overseas to commission the machine and we need them to travel here to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: So, with that, Minister, I just wanted to ask a supplementary question on this.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Between SIA and CAG, is there any leverage that the two can have to reduce the cost for SIA's planes parking on the tarmac?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But it is not a lot and not significant compared to all the costs of operating an airline because the planes are involved, huge number of workforce and we want to retain them as much as we can to maintain core capabilities.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, the overall fixed cost of maintaining SIA as a going concern, even when business is so far down, the cost is quite tremendous.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We do what we can and this is a crucial period in the next few months.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We hope by taking such steps, comprehensive, clear steps, no doubt there is a lot of uncertainty but the direction we want to go towards, what we can control and what we cannot control, we have a good sense of it.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will do our best to revive the air hub.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We want to ensure that when there is a vaccine, when air travel recovers again, we are right there and we are able to hold on to our position as an aviation hub.
